title: Sustainable style: How fashion can reduce Tier 2 emissions
summary: Tier 2 production (fabric manufacturing and treatment) accounts for 45-70% of fashion brands' Scope 3 emissions and represents the industry's biggest decarbonization opportunity. Two complementary routes exist: suppliers can implement technical decarbonization levers like renewable energy to achieve cost savings up to $250 per metric ton CO2e, while brands can incentivize lower-emission suppliers to cut emissions 20-50% without changing sourcing countries. Analysis of over 9,000 suppliers shows that up to 50% of Tier 2 emission reductions can be achieved near cost-neutrally, making this strategy more cost-efficient than relying solely on low-impact materials.
central_argument: Fashion brands can achieve significant cost-efficient decarbonization by working directly with fragmented Tier 2 suppliers through technical improvements and emission-intensity incentives rather than continuing to focus narrowly on low-impact material selection.
key_claims: Tier 2 production accounts for 45-70% of fashion brands' Scope 3 emissions
Up to 50% of Tier 2 emission abatement can be achieved in a near-cost-neutral way
Technical decarbonization levers can deliver cost savings of up to $250 per metric ton of CO2e
Brands can cut emissions by 20-50% by selecting suppliers with better emission profiles without changing manufacturing country of origin
Full decarbonization for an average-size Tier 2 cotton supplier costs approximately $30 per metric ton CO2e (1% cost increase)
Low-impact material selection is an insufficient and expensive decarbonization strategy compared to Tier 2 supplier engagement
Fashion brands typically lack direct relationships with Tier 2 suppliers due to fragmented supplier landscape
key_tensions: Current fashion industry focus on low-impact materials is insufficient and economically inefficient versus the demonstrated cost-effectiveness of Tier 2 supplier decarbonization
The complexity and fragmentation of Tier 2 supplier networks versus the necessity of direct brand engagement for emission reduction
Theoretical achievability of supplier decarbonization versus real-world implementation challenges that inflate costs 30-40% above projections
